svg.title: The 1024 ladder of memory units
svg.desc: Two ladders of memory units stand on one byte. First the binary rungs light up from the bottom, KiB, MiB, GiB, and TiB, each 1024 times the rung below, and each shows its power of two and its exact byte count. Next the decimal rungs appear beside them, kB, MB, GB, and TB, each 1000 times the rung below. Then a bar beside each pair grows to show how much more the binary unit holds: 2.4% at kilo, 4.9% at mega, 7.4% at giga, and 10.0% at tera. Last, the two tera rungs light up together, because a 1 TB disk holds only about 0.91 TiB.
svg.text: Binary units climb by 1024 and decimal units by 1000, so the binary unit pulls further ahead at every rung.
Binary units climb by 1024, the power of two closest to 1000: 1 KiB is 1024 bytes, and 1 MiB is 1024 KiB.
The decimal units beside them climb by 1000: 1 kB is 1000 bytes, and 1 MB is 1000 kB.
1024 is only 2.4% more than 1000, but the gap compounds at every rung, to about 10% at tera.
So a disk sold as 1 TB holds a trillion bytes, which is about 0.91 TiB.
Source: NIST, Prefixes for binary multiples: the IEC names and symbols, beside the SI prefixes they derive from.
